## Intent
Hypothesis: a branchless blend with per-particle hash RNG can approach the streaming ceiling by eliminating branch divergence and shared-state contention.

## Cache saturation
At N=4000 (already past the L1d spill at N≈963), ns/p is 10.333 at q=0.01 — per-particle overhead dominates at small N. Cost FALLS sharply to 5.904 ns/p at N=65000 (at the L2 spill, N≈61680) as overhead amortizes. Past the L2→DRAM spill the curve stays essentially FLAT: 5.862 at N=262000, rising only mildly to 6.154 at N=4M (q=0.01). There is no knee at the L2→DRAM transition, indicating the algo is not bandwidth-limited at large N. Death rate raises the floor without changing the N-shape: at q=0.25 the floor sits at ~8.4 ns/p across all N≥65000 versus ~5.9 at q=0.01, but the same flat-after-amortization profile holds. PMC data is unavailable, so cycle attribution cannot confirm the compute-bound interpretation directly.

## Bandwidth
Peak achieved is 11.6 GB/s at N=262000, q=0.01 — 46% of the 25.22 GB/s streaming ceiling. At q=0.05 the peak is 10.89 GB/s (43%); at q=0.25 it falls to 8.08 GB/s (32%). The algo is compute-bound: ns/p stays flat from N=65000 to N=4M despite crossing the L2→DRAM spill, which would not occur if memory were the limiter. The transition is by death rate, not by N — higher q activates a scalar scatter path that raises the compute floor from ~5.9 to ~8.4 ns/p. The algo never approaches the streaming ceiling in any measured regime.

## Assembly
The compiler partially vectorized across the components of a single particle, not across particles. The update path uses `fmul.4s`/`fadd.4s` on a 4-lane vector assembled via `ext.16b v21, v19, v20, #0xc` and `mov.s v21[3], v18[0]`, plus `fmul.2s`/`fadd.2s` on a 2-lane vector. A gather appears: `ld1.s {v20}[1], [x24]` loads one scalar element into a vector lane. The per-particle hash RNG is entirely scalar — a long `eor`/`mul`/`lsr`/`eor`/`mul`/`lsr` chain — and dominates the loop body. The main loop advances x15 by 0x44 (68 bytes) per iteration, confirming one-particle-at-a-time processing. The respawn path uses `ldrb`/`add`/`csel`/`strb` triplets with 0xff clamping for three color channels — pure scalar byte work. The scalar RNG chain explains the compute-bound 46% of ceiling; the byte-granular scatter explains the death-rate sensitivity.

## Verdict
Refuted — the algo never exceeds 46% of the streaming ceiling (11.6 GB/s at q=0.01, N=262000) because the per-particle scalar hash RNG makes it compute-bound, with ns/p flat at ~5.9 from N=65000 to N=4M despite the L2→DRAM spill. The branchless blend did not approach streaming; death rate raises the floor to 8.4 ns/p (q=0.25) via the scalar byte-granular scatter, further confirming compute, not bandwidth, is the limiter.
